statement: In adults who came to a hospital emergency department with chest pain after recent cocaine use, a heart attack (acute myocardial infarction) was diagnosed in a small minority, from under 1 to about 6 in 100 depending on the study. At one urban US hospital (Flint, Michigan, July 1996 to February 1998) whose policy was to admit every such patient for at least 23 hours, with cardiac enzymes on arrival and every 8 hours for 24 hours, 15 of 250 admitted adults (6%) met World Health Organization criteria for infarction on serial CK-MB testing; the 95% confidence interval is printed as 3.1% to 8.9% in the Results and as 4.1% to 8.9% in the abstract, and the exact interval is 3.4% to 9.7% (editors' calculation) (Weber et al., 2000). Patients entered if they reported cocaine use in the previous week or had a positive urine screen (185 of the 196 tested were positive); they were young (mean age 33.5 years), mostly men (77%), African American (84%) and smoked tobacco (77%), and most had used cocaine within the previous 24 hours, mostly by smoking crack. They were found through hospital records coded for cocaine or other drug use, urine testing was routine only for patients aged 50 or under without cardiac risk factors, records coded for infarction were searched more thoroughly than others, and 9 patients sent home from the emergency department were left out, all of which would tend to raise the share; the authors also cannot exclude that a few small infarctions were missed. In hospital there were 7 complications (sustained ventricular tachycardia in 2 patients, supraventricular tachycardia in 3, heart failure in 1 and a slow heart rhythm in 1), none more than 12 hours after arrival, and all 250 patients left hospital alive; no complication after 12 hours in 250 patients is compatible with a true rate of up to 1.5% (editors' calculation). The 2008 scientific statement of the American Heart Association (a consensus document without a systematic search; these figures are second-hand) reports infarction in 6% of 246 patients in the prospective multicentre COCHPA study and in the Weber series, in 2.8% of 218 patients in another series (which Weber et al. describe as 2.5% of 241), and in 0.7% of 293 patients in the prospective ACI-TIPI study, which enrolled people with a wider range of symptoms at urban, suburban and semirural hospitals, and it attributes part of the spread to who was enrolled and to diagnostic criteria; Weber et al. add, also second-hand, that retrospective series ranged from 0% to 31% depending on whom they enrolled. The statement also reports, second-hand, that in COCHPA an electrocardiogram showing ischaemia or infarction detected only 36% of infarctions (specificity 89.9%); that in a randomized observation-unit study of 344 patients, 10 of the 42 high-risk patients admitted directly (24%) had an infarction, while among lower-risk patients observed for 9 to 12 hours there were no cardiovascular deaths and 4 of 256 followed up (1.6% to 2%) had a non-fatal infarction within 30 days; and that among 130 patients with cocaine-associated infarction in a 29-hospital US series, 38% had complications, 90% of them within 12 hours, and none died in hospital (McCord et al., 2008). In that 29-hospital series (1987–1993; 136 infarctions in 130 patients, found through hospital records), no one died in hospital among the 66 patients whose first electrocardiogram met the criteria then used for clot-dissolving (thrombolytic) treatment; of the 25 who were given it, by their clinicians' decision, none had bleeding into the brain or bleeding that needed transfusion and two had minor complications, but with 25 patients a rate of such major complications of up to about 14% cannot be excluded (exact 95% interval 0 to 13.7%, editors' calculation; printed 0 to 12%), and patients who were given the treatment but turned out not to have an infarction were not included; adding 11 earlier case reports, the authors count one fatal bleed into the brain in 36 treated patients (Hollander et al., 1995). These figures describe people who reached hospital in the 1980s and 1990s, mostly young men in US cities and mostly tested with CK-MB enzymes, the standard of the time; they are not the chance of a heart attack each time a person uses cocaine, and none of these studies compared patients with chest pain who had not used cocaine.
plain: In studies of people who went to hospital with chest pain after using cocaine, about 1 to 6 in 100 were having a heart attack. At one US hospital that kept everyone with this problem in for a day of blood tests, it was 15 of 250 people (6 in 100); other hospital studies, as summed up by the American Heart Association, found from under 1 to 6 in 100, depending on who was included and how a heart attack was diagnosed. At that hospital, complications were few, none began more than 12 hours after arrival, and everyone left hospital alive; in another series of 130 people with a confirmed heart attack after cocaine, none died in hospital. In one study, a heart tracing (ECG) alone picked up only about a third of the heart attacks. These are older studies of people who reached hospital, mostly young men in US cities, and their blood tests could miss small heart attacks; they do not give anyone's chance of a heart attack each time they use cocaine.
population: Adults who came to hospital emergency departments with chest pain after recent cocaine use: all such patients admitted at one urban US hospital in 1996–1998 (read in full) and patients in other US emergency-department studies as summarized in the 2008 American Heart Association statement; and hospital patients with a confirmed cocaine-associated infarction at 29 US hospitals, 1987–1993
exposure: Recent cocaine use by history or urine test (within the previous week at the hospital read in full, mostly by smoking crack; within 24 hours in the 29-hospital series)
comparator: None for the share with infarction (no patients with chest pain who had not used cocaine); in the 29-hospital series, patients eligible for thrombolytic treatment who did not receive it
outcome: Acute myocardial infarction by the criteria of the time (WHO criteria with serial CK-MB in the study read in full); in-hospital complications and deaths; major bleeding after thrombolytic treatment
magnitude: Infarction among adults admitted with chest pain after recent cocaine use at one hospital: 15 of 250 (6%; printed 95% CI 3.1–8.9%, abstract 4.1–8.9%; exact 3.4–9.7%, editors' calculation). Other emergency-department studies, second-hand: 6% of 246 (COCHPA), 2.8% of 218 (2.5% of 241 in Weber et al.'s description of the same study), 0.7% of 293 (ACI-TIPI); range 0.7% to 6%. Observation-unit study, second-hand: infarction in 10 of 42 high-risk patients admitted directly (24%) and non-fatal infarction within 30 days in 4 of 256 lower-risk patients. In-hospital course at the one hospital: 7 complications in 250 patients, none after 12 hours (upper 95% limit 1.5%, editors' calculation), no deaths. Confirmed infarction (29-hospital series): no in-hospital deaths among 66 ECG-eligible patients; no major complication in 25 given thrombolytic treatment (exact 95% CI 0–13.7%, editors' calculation); complications in 38% of 130, 90% within 12 hours, in-hospital mortality 0% (second-hand). ECG sensitivity for infarction 36%, specificity 89.9% (COCHPA, second-hand).

Editors' calculation: 3.1–8.9% is the normal-approximation interval; the exact 95% interval for 15 of 250 is 3.4% to 9.7%. Of the 15, the first ECG was consistent with infarction in 9, ischaemic in 4 and normal or non-diagnostic in 2; 9 were Q-wave infarctions.

imprecision.note: 15 events in the study read in full give an exact interval of 3.4% to 9.7%; the thrombolysis observation (0 of 25) is imprecise and is reported with its interval rather than rated down.

(1995); Weber et al., COCHPA and the CAMI series share an investigator (J. E. Hollander), who was also on the AHA writing group. The figures describe people who reached hospital, not the risk of infarction per occasion of cocaine use, and no study compared patients with chest pain who had not used cocaine. The primary studies behind the second-hand figures (COCHPA, ACI-TIPI, Kontos et al., the observation-unit trial) have not been read.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether a beta-blocker given in hospital to people with chest pain after cocaine use makes the narrowing of the heart's arteries, heart attacks or deaths more likely. That cocaine itself narrows the coronary arteries and reduces blood flow to the heart muscle for a time was shown in a randomized, double-blind laboratory study of 30 patients undergoing cardiac catheterization for chest pain, none of whom had used cocaine before (Dallas, published 1990): 15 minutes after intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg (110 to 210 mg, a study condition the authors chose as one half to two thirds of the amount used for local anaesthesia of the nose and throat), against intranasal saline, systolic blood pressure rose by 11 mm Hg (95% CI 5 to 16), coronary sinus blood flow fell by 17 mL/min (5 to 29) and coronary vascular resistance rose, and six measured artery segments narrowed by 0.10 to 0.25 mm (about 6% to 10%, editors' calculation), significantly in four; no one had chest pain or electrocardiographic signs of ischaemia after cocaine alone (Lange et al., 1990). In a second study by the same group, the same dose reduced the area of disease-free artery segments by about 9% and 17% in its two arms (editors' calculation from the means; Boehrer et al., 1993). In the 1990 study, 10 of the patients given cocaine then received the beta-blocker propranolol infused directly into the left coronary artery (2 mg over 5 minutes): coronary sinus flow fell further, from 120 to 100 mL/min (change from the post-cocaine value −20 mL/min, 95% CI −42 to −1, P = 0.050), and resistance rose further (+0.16 mm Hg/mL per min, −0.02 to 0.33, P = 0.074), although the abstract reports P < 0.05 for both; nothing changed further in 5 patients given an intracoronary saline infusion after cocaine, nothing changed in 5 given propranolol after intranasal saline, and the randomized comparison between the two groups given cocaine was not tested. In 5 of the 10 an artery segment narrowed by more than 10%, and in one a coronary artery closed completely, with ischaemic symptoms and ST-segment elevation, which resolved after sublingual nitroglycerin without a rise in creatine kinase. In the 1993 study, intravenous labetalol (0.25 mg/kg), which blocks alpha as well as beta receptors, given to 9 such patients after cocaine lowered mean arterial pressure from 117 to 110 mm Hg but left the narrowed artery area unchanged (3.47 to 3.37 mm²); heart rate did not change at any point, so beta-blockade was not shown, allocation to labetalol or to saline (6 patients) was not described as randomized, and the two groups differed at baseline. Resting on these two studies (30 and 15 patients enrolled, of whom 10 and 9 received the blocker after cocaine; editors' count), on case reports and on animal experiments in which beta-blockers reduced coronary blood flow and increased seizures and deaths, the 2008 American Heart Association statement recommends that beta-blockers be avoided in the acute setting (Class III, Level of Evidence C, which it defines as consensus opinion of experts, case studies or standard of care), noting that no randomized trial of treatment for cocaine-associated infarction exists and that deaths from cocaine-associated infarction are very low, which alters the balance of risk and benefit; at discharge it reserves long-term beta-blockers for people with a documented infarction, a weakened left ventricle or ventricular arrhythmias, after counselling about cocaine use (McCord et al., 2008). In practice, 164 of 376 patients (44%) admitted with chest pain and a cocaine-positive urine screen at two St Louis hospitals in 2000–2007 were given a beta-blocker within 24 hours (metoprolol 74, labetalol 44, carvedilol 43, atenolol 3, so 87 received a drug that also blocks alpha receptors); they were older, had more hypertension and coronary disease, and received more aspirin, nitrates and other cardiac drugs, which were not adjusted for. In-hospital myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia or death occurred in 16% of them and 12% of the others (odds ratio adjusted for propensity-score quintile 1.37, 95% CI 0.64 to 2.93); myocardial infarction in 5% against 2% (1.67, 0.44 to 6.35) and death in 3% against 6% (0.66, 0.14 to 3.04); the odds ratio was 1.83 (0.79 to 4.24) for beta-1-selective drugs and 0.90 (0.33 to 2.42) for carvedilol or labetalol, not tested against each other (Fanari et al., 2014). A meta-analysis of five retrospective US cohorts (1756 patients; 1794 in its abstract), pooling unadjusted counts, found no significant difference: non-fatal myocardial infarction in 94 of 610 patients (15.4%) given a beta-blocker and 162 of 1146 (14.1%) not given one (odds ratio 1.36, 0.68 to 2.74; I² 71%, single cohorts ranging from 0.18, 0.04 to 0.79, to 3.14, 1.42 to 6.95), and death in 6 of 348 (1.7%) against 22 of 666 (3.3%) (0.68, 0.26 to 1.79; three cohorts). It entered Fanari et al.'s percentages as event counts (5 and 2 for infarction, 3 and 6 for death); with the counts those percentages imply (about 8 of 164 and 4 of 212; 5 of 164 and 13 of 212) the pooled odds ratios are about 1.38 (0.70 to 2.69) for infarction and 0.56 (0.24 to 1.28) for death, still not significant (editors' calculation, which reproduces the printed results exactly from the printed counts). Its text attributes the one significant increase in infarction to the cohort that found a significant decrease, and it describes the two laboratory studies as giving 45 people intravenous beta-blockers (Pham et al., 2018). The laboratory studies measured artery size and blood flow for minutes after one moderate dose in people who had never used cocaine, with propranolol infused into a coronary artery rather than given by vein or by mouth; the hospital cohorts could not tell whether cocaine was still active when the drug was given (urine screens stay positive for 2 to 3 days), gave the drug to sicker patients, mixed drugs with and without alpha-blocking action, and had too few events to exclude either harm or benefit. No randomized trial has compared beta-blockers with other treatments in people with chest pain after cocaine.
plain: In a hospital laboratory, one moderate dose of cocaine sniffed by heart patients who had never used it narrowed their heart arteries a little and cut blood flow to the heart muscle for a time; a dummy dose did nothing. When 10 of them were then given the beta-blocker propranolol straight into a heart artery, blood flow fell further, and in one person an artery closed until doctors gave nitroglycerin; this did not happen with a dummy infusion, or with propranolol given without cocaine. Labetalol, which blocks alpha as well as beta receptors, lowered blood pressure in 9 such patients but did not widen their narrowed arteries. Mainly on these small studies, the American Heart Association advised in 2008 against beta-blockers soon after cocaine use, grading this as expert opinion. Hospital records have not shown this harm: among about 1,750 patients with chest pain and cocaine in their urine, heart attacks and deaths were not clearly more or less common in those given a beta-blocker. But doctors gave it to sicker people, nobody knew whether the cocaine was still active, and a review of these records copied some numbers wrongly (correcting them does not change its result). No trial has tested beta-blockers in people with chest pain after cocaine, so whether they make things worse is not known. See the contested question.
population: Patients undergoing cardiac catheterization for chest pain who had never used cocaine (two laboratory studies by one Dallas group: 30 and 15 patients); patients admitted with chest pain and a cocaine-positive urine screen at US hospitals (five retrospective cohorts, 1998–2011, pooled in one meta-analysis; one of them, 376 patients in St Louis, read in full)
exposure: In the laboratory, intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg (study condition) followed by propranolol infused into the left coronary artery (2 mg) or intravenous labetalol (0.25 mg/kg); in hospitals, any beta-blocker given in routine care (in the cohort read in full, within 24 hours: metoprolol, labetalol, carvedilol or atenolol)
comparator: In the laboratory, intranasal saline, a saline infusion after cocaine, and propranolol after intranasal saline; in hospitals, patients with cocaine-associated chest pain not given a beta-blocker
outcome: Coronary blood flow, coronary vascular resistance and artery size (laboratory); in-hospital myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia and death (hospital records)
magnitude: Not estimable as an effect of beta-blockers on clinical outcomes. debate.question: Does a beta-blocker given in hospital to someone with chest pain after cocaine narrow the heart's arteries further and make heart attacks or deaths more likely?
debate.evidence_yes: In the one randomized laboratory study, propranolol infused into the left coronary artery of 10 catheterization patients 15 minutes after intranasal cocaine was followed by a further fall in coronary blood flow (120 to 100 mL/min, P = 0.050 against the post-cocaine value) and a further rise in resistance (P = 0.074), changes not seen in 5 patients given a saline infusion after cocaine or in 5 given propranolol without cocaine; 5 of the 10 had an artery segment narrow by more than 10%, and one had a complete coronary occlusion with ischaemic symptoms and ST-segment elevation (Lange et al., 1990). The explanation offered, that blocking beta receptors leaves cocaine's stimulation of alpha receptors in the arteries unopposed, underlies the American Heart Association's 2008 Class III recommendation to avoid beta-blockers in the acute setting, which also cites animal experiments in which beta-blockers decreased coronary blood flow and increased seizures and deaths, and reports, second-hand, that the short-acting beta-1 blocker esmolol raised blood pressure significantly in up to 25% of patients (McCord et al., 2008). Among the hospital cohorts, one (Mohamad et al., 2008, as shown in the meta-analysis's forest plot) found myocardial infarction more often with a beta-blocker (odds ratio 3.14, 1.42 to 6.95), and the pooled infarction estimate points the same way (1.36, upper limit 2.74; about 1.38 with Fanari et al.'s counts corrected, editors' calculation) (Pham et al., 2018). In the cohort read in full, the point estimates for the composite outcome (1.37) and for infarction (1.67) are above 1, and beta-1-selective drugs gave 1.83 against 0.90 for drugs that also block alpha receptors, the pattern the unopposed-alpha explanation predicts, though the difference was not tested (Fanari et al., 2014).
debate.evidence_no: No study has measured a clinical outcome of beta-blockers after cocaine in a randomized comparison. In hospital records, beta-blockers were often given despite the guidance (to 44% of 376 patients with cocaine-positive chest pain at two hospitals in 2000–2007), and the patients who received one, although older and with more heart disease, did not have detectably more in-hospital infarction, stroke, arrhythmia or death after adjustment for a propensity score (odds ratio 1.37, 0.64 to 2.93); deaths were fewer (3% against 6%; 0.66, 0.14 to 3.04) (Fanari et al., 2014). Pooling five such cohorts (1756 patients) gave no significant difference in non-fatal infarction (1.36, 0.68 to 2.74) or death (0.68, 0.26 to 1.79, three cohorts; about 0.56, 0.24 to 1.28, with Fanari et al.'s counts corrected, editors' calculation); one cohort (Dattilo et al., 2008) found infarction less often with a beta-blocker (0.18, 0.04 to 0.79), and the authors, one of whom also wrote the 2008 statement, conclude that the guidelines should be reconsidered (Pham et al., 2018). The laboratory case for harm is narrow: 19 people received a blocker after cocaine in the two studies, none of whom had used cocaine before; propranolol went directly into a coronary artery at one dose; the rise in resistance after propranolol did not reach the authors' own threshold against the post-cocaine value (P = 0.074), the randomized comparison was not tested, and no clinical outcome was measured (Lange et al., 1990). Labetalol, which also blocks alpha receptors, did not narrow the arteries further in 9 patients and lowered blood pressure (Boehrer et al., 1993). The AHA statement grades its recommendation Level of Evidence C and marks no clinical trial or observational study behind it (McCord et al., 2008).
debate.neither_can_show: The laboratory studies measured artery size, blood flow and resistance for minutes after one moderate intranasal dose in cardiac patients who had never used cocaine, so they cannot show what happens to people who use cocaine, at the amounts they use, when a beta-blocker is given by vein or by mouth, or whether any heart attack or death follows. The hospital cohorts cannot show it either: doctors chose whom to treat and chose sicker patients, who also received more aspirin, nitrates and other heart drugs that were not adjusted for; the beta-blocker was recorded over the first 24 hours while events were counted over the whole stay, so people who had an early event may have been less likely to get the drug; urine screens stay positive for days, so whether cocaine was still active when the drug was given is unknown; the drugs given were a mix of beta-1-selective drugs and drugs that also block alpha receptors, which the meta-analysis could not separate; and with about 52 events in the cohort read in full and 28 deaths in the pooled analysis of death, the intervals include both appreciable harm and appreciable benefit. The meta-analysis pooled unadjusted counts, with a data-entry error in one cohort.
debate.editors_reading: The editors' reading: that cocaine narrows the coronary arteries and lowers coronary blood flow in the minutes after use is shown in a randomized laboratory comparison, though in a small, selected group (people who had never used cocaine, given one moderate dose). Whether a beta-blocker given in hospital makes outcomes worse is not known. A plausible mechanism, seen in 10 people given propranolol into a coronary artery, points to harm; hospital records of about 1,750 patients neither show nor exclude harm, with estimates on both sides of no effect. Certainty is very low. The AHA's Class III recommendation is expert consensus resting on the laboratory studies, not on outcomes in patients; the meta-analysis's suggestion that beta-blockers may be safe rests on unadjusted, confounded and partly misentered data. The evidence read settles neither the recommendation nor its reversal.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in people who come to hospital with chest pain after recent, confirmed cocaine use, comparing an intravenous beta-blocker (beta-1-selective and combined alpha-beta blockers separately) with the currently recommended treatments (a benzodiazepine or nitroglycerin), with blinded assessment of infarction, arrhythmia and death and enough events to exclude a meaningful difference. Short of that, an individual-patient analysis of the existing cohorts using adjusted estimates, the timing of the drug relative to events, and separation by drug type.

statement: As described in two narrative reviews (Buchanan & Lavonas, 2012; Roberts & Chévez-Barrios, 2015; no systematic search or appraisal; all figures second-hand), levamisole, a veterinary medicine used mainly against worms in cattle, sheep and pigs and formerly used in people for autoimmune conditions and some cancers, was found in much of the cocaine sold in the United States around 2010: the US Drug Enforcement Administration first detected it in seized cocaine in 2003 and, by a figure the review does not source, in 73.2% of the cocaine it analysed in January 2010; in seizures in Luxembourg it was the commonest adulterant, at 1.5% to 4.1% of the sample; studies published in 2011 found it in 78% (Denver) and 88% (San Francisco) of urine samples from hospital patients that screened positive for cocaine metabolites; and the later review states that about 70% of US cocaine contains it. Case reports and small series from 2009 onward, first from Alberta, British Columbia, New Mexico, Washington, Arizona and Colorado, describe two conditions in people who had smoked, injected or snorted cocaine. One is agranulocytosis, an almost complete loss of the neutrophil white blood cells that fight infection, most often after smoking: neutrophil counts recovered within about 2 to 3 days of hospital treatment with GCSF in most case reports and within about 5 to 10 days after exposure ended without it, and about half of the patients in one series had more than one episode when they used cocaine again. The other is a skin vasculopathy: painful purple patches in a net-like or star-shaped pattern, sometimes with blisters and dead skin, typically on the ears, cheeks, nose and limbs, with autoantibodies (such as ANCA), clotted small vessels and/or inflamed vessel walls on biopsy, and neutropenia in about half of cases; women made up most of the reported cases although more men use cocaine. The lesions usually resolved within a few weeks after cocaine use stopped, though some patients needed removal of dead tissue, skin grafts or amputation; no treatment has been tested in a controlled study. The cases were attributed to levamisole mainly from their pattern, from the person's cocaine use (by history or a urine test for a cocaine metabolite) and from the same effects seen when levamisole was used as a medicine: the first in-depth case report with laboratory confirmation of levamisole appeared in early 2010; levamisole leaves the blood within about a day (plasma half-life about 5.6 hours, a figure the earlier review does not source) and stays detectable in urine for about 2 to 3 days; and the later review states that testing for it is not needed for diagnosis because it is so common in cocaine, so cases were often attributed without measuring it, and since most people who use cocaine would test positive, a positive test shows exposure rather than cause. A brain disorder (leukoencephalopathy) was linked to levamisole as a medicine, but the earlier review reports that no case acquired through cocaine had been reported, although its summary lists it among the consequences. Neither review gives how often these conditions occur among people exposed to levamisole through cocaine or weighs cocaine itself as a cause; the earlier review's statement that a significant minority of exposed people will be affected has no number behind it, and the later review's statement that the incidence is rising has no data behind it.
plain: Levamisole is a medicine used to treat worms in farm animals that was once also used in people. Around 2010 it was found in about 7 in 10 samples of cocaine tested by US drug police, and in the urine of about 8 or 9 in 10 hospital patients whose urine tested positive for cocaine in two US cities. Since 2009, case reports have described two kinds of harm in people who used cocaine. In some, the white blood cells that fight infection almost disappeared; the counts came back about 5 to 10 days after the exposure stopped, or within 2 to 3 days with a medicine given in hospital, and about half of the people in one series had it happen again when they used cocaine again. Others had painful purple patches on the skin, sometimes with dying skin, often on the ears, cheeks, nose, arms or legs; most healed within a few weeks after cocaine use stopped, but some people needed skin grafts or an amputation. These cases were linked to levamisole mainly because the person had used cocaine and because the same problems were seen when levamisole was a medicine; levamisole itself was often not tested for. How often this harm happens to people exposed to levamisole is not known: the sources are case reports, described second-hand in two reviews.

statement: In seven cohorts of people with problematic or dependent cocaine use, followed between 1985 and 2005 in the USA (two cohorts), Canada, France, the Netherlands, Brazil and Italy and summarized without pooling in one systematic review (Degenhardt et al., 2011; figures second-hand, several of them supplied by the cohorts' investigators as personal communications), deaths were 4.4 to 7.7 times as frequent as in the general population of the same age and sex in the four cohorts that reported standardized mortality ratios (SMR): 4.74 (95% CI 4.19 to 5.29) among 717 people injecting cocaine in Vancouver; 4.36 among men and 7.70 among women in a French national cohort of 2212 people arrested for using or dealing cocaine or crack; 4.75 (2.26 to 9.96) among men in treatment for cocaine dependence in Italy (mostly intranasal use by one of the review's two descriptions, crack dependence by the other); and 7.60 at five years among 131 people treated for crack dependence in São Paulo. Crude death rates ranged from about 0.5 to 6.2 per 100 person-years, that is about 5 to 62 deaths per 1,000 people per year: 6.16 in the Vancouver cohort; 4.69 among people injecting cocaine only and 4.37 among people injecting cocaine and heroin in Baltimore; 4.6 among HIV-negative people mainly injecting cocaine in the Netherlands (9 deaths); 3.51 in the São Paulo crack cohort and 3.53 among people smoking crack daily in Seattle (3 deaths); and 0.69 in the French arrest cohort and 0.50 in the Italian treatment cohort. Where it was examined, death rates were about twice as high in people with HIV (Vancouver 9.83 against 4.91 per 100 person-years; Baltimore 7.74 and 7.98 against 3.25 and 3.45). The leading causes of death were AIDS, overdose and injuries among people who injected (Baltimore, people injecting cocaine only: AIDS 62 of 175 deaths, overdose 20, sepsis or endocarditis 15, injuries 12, heart disease 7, suicide 2; Vancouver: overdose 53, AIDS 30 and injuries 23 of 158 deaths), gunshot wounds (10 of 23 deaths) and AIDS (6) among people treated for crack dependence in Brazil, and, in the Italian cohort of 309 men with 7 deaths, cause-specific SMRs of 14.85 (4.79 to 46.04) for vascular disease, 9.95 (1.40 to 70.61) for overdose and 7.07 (1 to 50.16) for suicide. The SMRs take only age and sex into account, so they describe the excess deaths in these groups, not an effect of cocaine itself apart from injecting, HIV, heroin and alcohol use and social disadvantage, which the authors name as possible reasons for the differences. All the cohorts came from injecting, treatment or arrest settings, mostly socially disadvantaged and several with high HIV prevalence, the effect of HIV treatment could not be examined, and no cohort followed people who only snort cocaine (the authors think it likely, citing another study, that their mortality is much lower, but there are no data). How deaths were identified and causes assigned is not reported for the cohorts, and the review's table has inconsistencies: the lowest crude rate printed (0.53, for people injecting daily in Seattle) does not match its own 3 deaths in 319 person-years, which give 0.94 (editors' calculation).

In the four groups compared with the general population of the same age and sex, 4 to 8 times as many died as expected. Among people who injected, the main causes were AIDS, overdose and injuries; among people treated for crack dependence in Brazil, gunshot wounds and AIDS. Many people in these groups also injected heroin or had HIV, and the comparison took only age and sex into account, so these figures do not show what cocaine itself does. No group of people who only snort cocaine has been followed. The figures come from one review that did not combine them, and some were sent by the researchers rather than published.

statement: In people with lifetime cocaine use seen in treatment settings (17 studies, 5286 people, almost all in outpatient drug treatment services, with one inpatient service and one psychiatric emergency unit; 13 of all 20 included studies from the USA, 4 from Spain and one each from Canada, Brazil and the French Caribbean; mean age 37, 68% men; people with primary psychotic disorders excluded), one meta-analysis of studies published to August 2020 found that how common cocaine-induced psychosis is depends on how it is defined (Sabe et al., 2021). In 13 studies that asked about psychotic symptoms with cocaine (questionnaires such as the Cocaine Experience Questionnaire, which mainly asks about paranoia and also about hallucinations, or study-specific questions, in two studies a single symptom), a pooled 68.4% (95% CI 62.8 to 73.5; I² 89%) reported having had them; in 4 studies that used diagnostic interviews (PRISM or MINI) for a DSM cocaine-induced psychotic disorder, 16% (10.6 to 23.2; I² 89%; 8.5 to 28.3 with a between-study variance estimated within that subgroup alone, editors' calculation) met the criteria; by instrument the figures ranged from 11.7% (PRISM, 3 studies) to 84.2% (SAPS-CIP, 1 study), and by region from 25.1% in Europe to 66.5% in North America. The single pooled lifetime figure of 55.6% combines these definitions (I² 97%), and its printed interval (50.2 to 61.0) is narrower than a standard random-effects interval (46.0 to 64.8; editors' calculation). The figure for current use (50.2%, 32.0 to 68.4) rests on 102 people in three studies, two of them laboratory studies in which 12 of 28 and 29 of 44 volunteers reported paranoia while taking cocaine in a research unit and one a psychiatric emergency series (12 of 30), so it is not a prevalence among people who currently use cocaine. Other drug use was common where reported (lifetime dependence on alcohol 56.5% in 3 studies, cannabis 32% and opioids 30% in 2) and could not be separated from cocaine, and neither could amount or route; the authors state that cocaine cannot be shown to be directly responsible, that treatment samples may inflate the figures (selection and Berkson bias) while people's limited insight into their symptoms may deflate them, and that cross-sectional studies with mostly retrospective assessment cannot show cause. Two reports with identical counts may count the same 243 people twice (without one of them, 67.7% for symptoms, editors' calculation), and two studies, including the largest (2192 people), have no entry in the reference list. The review states, citing other work, that such symptoms are usually transient and pass with abstinence, and that a 2020 meta-analysis found no study of how often cocaine-induced psychotic disorder turns into schizophrenia; it did not measure either itself. A corrigendum to this review was published (Sabe et al., 2022, doi:10.1016/j.pnpbp.2021.110434) but has not been read, because the file saved under its name is a different document; it might correct the missing abstract, the reference list, the possibly duplicated study or the pooled figures themselves, so every figure here is provisional until it is read.
plain: The answer depends on how psychosis is measured. In a review of 17 studies of 5,286 people, mostly in treatment for cocaine use in the USA and Spain, about 68 in 100 said that cocaine had at some time given them psychotic symptoms, such as paranoia, when asked with questionnaires; when strict diagnostic interviews were used, about 16 in 100 had a cocaine-induced psychotic disorder. Figures were lower in the European studies than in the North American ones. Many of these people were also dependent on alcohol or other drugs, which the review could not separate from cocaine, so it cannot show that cocaine alone caused the symptoms; and people in treatment may differ from others who use cocaine. The review says, citing other work, that such symptoms usually pass when cocaine use stops, and that no study has measured how often a cocaine-induced psychotic disorder turns into schizophrenia; it did not study either itself. A correction to the review has been published, but we have not read it yet; it might change these figures.

risk_of_bias.note: Cross-sectional studies in treatment samples, mostly with retrospective self-report of symptoms (selection and Berkson bias named by the authors); two reports may count the same 243 people twice; the review is of critically low confidence on AMSTAR 2 (card sc_sabe_2021) and its corrigendum has not been read.

inconsistency.note: I² 89% within each definition and 97% overall; figures differ by instrument (11.7% to 84.2%) and by region (Europe 25.1%, North America 66.5%), largely unexplained.

indirectness.note: Treatment samples, mostly in the USA and Spain, not people who use cocaine in general; other drug use was common and could not be separated, so the symptoms are attributed to cocaine by the people asked or by the interviewer.

imprecision.note: The definition-specific intervals are moderately narrow; the overall printed interval understates the spread (editors' calculation) and is not used as the headline figure.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review; not rated down, because prevalence studies are unlikely to be published according to the prevalence they find.

grade.reasoning: Prevalence figures are descriptive (relation 'describes') and start low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness, which is below the floor: very low. Status replicated: within each definition, independent studies agree in order of magnitude (13 symptom studies, prediction interval about 48% to 84%, editors' calculation; 4 diagnostic studies, 10% to 36%), the spread being rated under inconsistency; Cubells 2005 and Tang 2007 may be one sample and are counted once. The current-use figure is not used as a prevalence. Every figure is provisional until the published corrigendum (Sabe et al., 2022) is read; the primary studies, the review's supplementary tables and the 2020 meta-analysis on transition (card sc_murrie_2020, on the methamphetamine page) were not used here.
